title: Your First Script
story:
It is 8:55 on your first morning at Lanternfish Hosting. The harbour fog is
still on the windows, the coffee machine is gurgling, and Mara has pulled a
chair up to your desk. "Before I show you the servers," she says, "make the
terminal say hello. Every engineer here started with exactly this."
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly this one line:
  Hello, Lanternfish!
The file already starts with a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env bash). Keep it,
and add one command underneath that prints the greeting.
concepts: echo prints a line of text

required_patterns.message: Use the echo command to print the greeting.

title: Two Lines of Output
story:
Ollie, the intern, is on the night shift and keeps forgetting the handover
routine. Mara's fix: a tiny script that prints the handover note, so Ollie
only has to type one command. The note is three lines, and the order matters
because people read it top to bottom with a sleepy brain.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly these three lines, in this order:
  HANDOVER NOTE
  Pager: Ollie
  Coffee: refilled
Use a separate echo command for each line.
concepts: commands run top to bottom, so output order follows script order

required_patterns.message: Use three echo commands, one for each line of the note.

test_cases.name: handover note
test_cases.expected_stdout:
HANDOVER NOTE
Pager: Ollie
Coffee: refilled

title: Quotes Keep Your Spaces
story:
Noor from the support desk wants a little sign printed on the shared
terminal for the Gull & Anchor Pub's rack: three words with wide gaps so
the pub's landlord can read it from across the room. Theo tried it with a
plain echo and the gaps vanished. "It just squashed everything!" he said.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly this line, including the wide
gaps (three spaces between each pair of words):
  GULL   AND   ANCHOR
Use double quotes so the spaces survive.
concepts: double quotes keep the text together as one argument
without quotes Bash collapses runs of spaces into one

required_patterns.message: Put the whole sign inside double quotes, e.g. echo "...", so the gaps are kept.

title: Single Quotes Are Literal
story:
Priya is writing the security reminder that pops up when someone logs in to
a Lanternfish server. It has to mention the names of shell variables, $HOME
and $USER, as plain words, because new hires keep pasting their real values
into support tickets. Her first attempt printed a path instead of the word
$HOME, which rather defeated the point.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly these two lines, with the dollar
signs as ordinary characters:
  Never paste $HOME or $USER into a ticket.
  Late report fee: $5 per day.
Use single quotes so Bash leaves every character alone.
concepts: single quotes: no expansion at all

required_patterns.message: Wrap the text in single quotes, e.g. echo '...$...', so the $ signs stay literal.

test_cases.name: dollar signs survive
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Never paste $HOME or $USER into a ticket.
Late report fee: $5 per day.

title: Escapes with printf
story:
Gus wants a quick table of which servers are up so he can paste it straight
into his spreadsheet. Spreadsheets split columns on tab characters, and a
row of spaces will not do. Mara introduces you to printf, the careful
cousin of echo, which understands \t for a tab and \n for a new line.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that a single printf command prints this table. The
gaps are real tab characters and each row ends with a newline:
  SERVER<TAB>STATUS
  anchovy<TAB>up
  barracuda<TAB>down
Use \t and \n inside the printf text; do not type literal tabs.
concepts: printf does not add a newline on its own
\n is a new line, \t is a tab

required_patterns.message: Use printf for this one.
Use \t for the tab characters.
Use \n to end each row.

forbidden_patterns.message: This level is about printf; leave echo out.

test_cases.name: tab separated table
test_cases.expected_stdout:
SERVER	STATUS
anchovy	up
barracuda	down

title: printf Placeholders
story:
Noor's support desk tool drops three values into the environment before it
calls your script: CUSTOMER (the business name, which may contain spaces),
TICKETS (how many tickets are open) and OLDEST (the number of the oldest
one). She wants one summary line for the wall dashboard, and she wants the
numbers to stay numbers: no surprises if a customer's name is long.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints one line in this exact shape:
  Customer: <CUSTOMER> | open: <TICKETS> | oldest: #<OLDEST>
For example: Customer: North Pier Dental | open: 4 | oldest: #1180
The values are in the variables $CUSTOMER, $TICKETS and $OLDEST. Write them
inside double quotes ("$CUSTOMER") so names with spaces stay in one piece.
Use one printf with %s for the name and %d for each number.

required_patterns.message: Use printf here.
Use %s for the customer name.
Use %d for the numbers.

test_cases.name: dental practice
test_cases.expected_stdout: Customer: North Pier Dental | open: 4 | oldest: #1180

test_cases.name: nothing open
test_cases.expected_stdout: Customer: Gull & Anchor Pub | open: 0 | oldest: #0

title: Padding Columns
story:
Gus prints the daily "who is on which server" sheet and pins it to the
kitchen fridge. Last week the numbers wandered left and right like boats at
low tide, and he squinted for ten minutes. He asks for tidy columns: names
flush left in a fixed-width box, numbers flush right in another. The
monitoring tool sets HOST and USERS before it calls you.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints two lines. The brackets make the padding
visible, so keep them:
  [HOST      ] [USERS]
  [<HOST padded to 10, left-aligned>] [<USERS padded to 5, right-aligned>]
For HOST=dory and USERS=42 the second line is:  [dory      ] [   42]
Use printf with %-10s (left, width 10) and %5d (right, width 5) for the data
line. The header line uses the same widths: [%-10s] [%5s].
Read the values from $HOST and $USERS, in double quotes.

required_patterns.message: Use %-10s to pad the host name to 10 characters, left-aligned.
Use %5d to right-align the user count in 5 characters.

title: No Trailing Newline
story:
The nightly backup check takes a few seconds per step, and Mara likes to
watch it work: first the label appears, then, when the step finishes, the
verdict lands on the same line. "Like a ship's log," she says. For that, the
label must not end the line. The step's verdict arrives in the environment
as RESULT (for example ok or FAILED).
objective:
Write solution.sh so that the output is one single line:
  Checking backups... <RESULT>
For RESULT=ok that is:  Checking backups... ok
Print the label "Checking backups... " (with a space at the end) in one
command that does not add a newline, then print $RESULT in a second command
that does end the line. Use echo -n or printf without \n for the first one.
concepts: printf only prints a newline if you write \n

required_patterns.message: Use two commands: one prints the label, a second prints the result.
Print the label with echo -n or with printf and no \n.

title: Talking to stderr
story:
Every night a cron job emails whatever the sync script prints to the
customer, and last Tuesday the Harbour Bakery received "WARNING: spare disk
almost full" in their inbox. Priya was not amused. The fix is to keep the
customer's report and the team's warnings in separate channels. The tool
sets HOST to the machine being synced.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints two messages, each to its own stream.
To standard output (the report for the customer):
  report: nightly sync complete on <HOST>
To standard error (the warning for the team):
  warning: <HOST> is using the spare disk
Read the machine name from $HOST. Send the warning to stderr by adding
>&2 to its command.
concepts: >&2 sends a command's output to stderr

required_patterns.message: Send the warning to stderr by ending its command with >&2.

test_cases.name: marlin
test_cases.expected_stdout: report: nightly sync complete on marlin
test_cases.expected_stderr: warning: marlin is using the spare disk

test_cases.name: octopus
test_cases.expected_stdout: report: nightly sync complete on octopus
test_cases.expected_stderr: warning: octopus is using the spare disk

test_cases.name: name with a dash
test_cases.expected_stdout: report: nightly sync complete on sea-urchin-2
test_cases.expected_stderr: warning: sea-urchin-2 is using the spare disk

title: Comments Are for Humans
story:
Theo left a cache warm-up script for Tidewater Books on the shared drive,
with his debugging echo lines still switched on. Mara opens it, sighs
gently, and hands it to you: "Quiet the noise, but do not delete anything.
Next month someone will want those debug lines back, and that someone might
be you. And give the file a proper name tag at the top."
objective:
Edit solution.sh so that it prints only these two lines:
  Warming the cache for Tidewater Books
  Cache warm: 3 pages
Silence the two lines that start with echo "DEBUG by turning them into
comments (put # in front of each), do not delete them.
Then add a header block of comments right under the shebang line with two
lines that begin exactly like this:
  # Purpose: <what the script does>
  # Author: <your name>
concepts: # starts a comment; Bash ignores the rest of the line
commenting out code instead of deleting it

test_cases.name: only the real output remains
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Warming the cache for Tidewater Books
Cache warm: 3 pages

title: Exit Codes Speak
story:
The monitoring wall at Lanternfish is run by a small program that never
reads what your script prints. It only looks at the number your script
returns when it finishes: 0 means fine, 1 means a warning, 2 means call
somebody. Ollie wrote the order-queue check and it always reports "fine",
even when the queue is backed up all the way to the pier.
objective:
Edit solution.sh so that it prints exactly this one line to standard output:
  CRITICAL: order queue is backed up
and then ends immediately with exit status 2. The echo "all clear" line
that is already in the file must never run, so the script has to stop
before reaching it.
concepts: exit N ends the script with status N
0 means success, anything else means a problem

required_patterns.message: End the script with exit 2.

test_cases.name: critical state
test_cases.expected_stdout: CRITICAL: order queue is backed up

title: Reading the Environment
story:
The shared jump box is where half the team logs in, and Ollie has twice run
a clean-up command while logged in as the wrong person. Mara wants a tiny
"who am I" script that every login prints, so nobody has to wonder. Your
shell already knows the answer: it keeps it in environment variables.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly one line:
  You are <USER>, your home folder is <HOME>
where <USER> and <HOME> are the values of the environment variables $USER
and $HOME. For USER=noor and HOME=/home/noor that is:
  You are noor, your home folder is /home/noor
Do not type the names or paths yourself; read them from the environment.

required_patterns.message: Read the user name from $USER.
Read the home folder from $HOME.

test_cases.name: noor
test_cases.expected_stdout: You are noor, your home folder is /home/noor

test_cases.name: root
test_cases.expected_stdout: You are root, your home folder is /root

test_cases.name: odd characters
test_cases.expected_stdout: You are mara.k, your home folder is /srv/people/mara k

title: Command Substitution
story:
Noor keeps the support queue in a plain text file, one ticket per line, with
the oldest ticket on top and the newest at the bottom. Every morning she
opens it just to learn two things: what has been waiting longest, and what
came in last. She asks you for a script that answers both and hands the
results to the dashboard, so she can keep her coffee warm.
objective:
The queue file is fixtures/queue.txt. Write solution.sh so that it prints
two lines:
  Oldest: <first line of the file>
  Newest: <last line of the file>
Let commands fetch the lines for you: head -n 1 FILE prints the first line
and tail -n 1 FILE prints the last. Put each of them inside $( ... ) in
your echo text. If the file has only one line, both lines show it.
concepts: $(command) is replaced by the command's output

required_patterns.message: Use command substitution, $(command), to fetch the lines.

test_cases.name: three tickets
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Oldest: T-5021 printer jam at Harbour Bakery
Newest: T-5023 password reset, North Pier Dental

test_cases.name: a different queue

files.fixtures/queue.txt:
T-6001 DNS question, Gull & Anchor Pub
T-6002 backup restore
T-6003 invoice copy
T-6004 new mailbox

test_cases.expected_stdout:
Oldest: T-6001 DNS question, Gull & Anchor Pub
Newest: T-6004 new mailbox

test_cases.name: only one ticket
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Oldest: T-7001 lost password
Newest: T-7001 lost password

title: The Script Knows Its Name
story:
Theo renames his scripts as often as other people change socks, and the
help messages keep saying the old names: "usage: old-backup-final-v2.sh".
Mara wants a script that never lies about itself. The nightly tool also
tells it where its report was written, as a full path in REPORT_PATH, but
the log wants just the file name, not the whole directory trail.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints exactly two lines:
  This script is called <script name>
  Report file: <file name part of $REPORT_PATH>
When run as bash solution.sh with REPORT_PATH=/var/reports/2024/nightly.txt:
  This script is called solution.sh
  Report file: nightly.txt
Get the script's own name from $0 and use the basename command to strip
folders from a path; the name must not be typed by hand.
concepts: $0 holds the name the script was started with
basename strips the directory part of a path

required_patterns.message: Read the script's name from $0.
Use basename to drop the folders from a path.

test_cases.name: nightly report
test_cases.expected_stdout:
This script is called solution.sh
Report file: nightly.txt

test_cases.name: report in the current folder
test_cases.expected_stdout:
This script is called solution.sh
Report file: weekly.csv

test_cases.name: folder with spaces
test_cases.expected_stdout:
This script is called solution.sh
Report file: Q3 totals.txt

title: Here-Document Banner
story:
Before every maintenance window Lanternfish sends the customer a short
notice. Noor has been pasting it from a document, and last week a notice
went out with the previous customer's name in it. Mara wants the notice
generated by a script, with the customer and the time slot filled in from
the environment as CUSTOMER and WINDOW. Seven echo lines would work, but
Mara says there is a nicer way.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints this notice, with <CUSTOMER> and
<WINDOW> replaced by the values of $CUSTOMER and $WINDOW:
  Dear <CUSTOMER>,
  (blank line)
  We will be doing maintenance on your server during:
      <WINDOW>
  Your sites may be unavailable for a few minutes.
  (blank line)
  -- Lanternfish Hosting
The line with the time slot starts with four spaces. Produce it with a
single cat <<EOF ... EOF here-document, not with several echo commands.
concepts: variables expand inside an unquoted here-document

required_patterns.message: Use a here-document: cat <<EOF ... EOF.

forbidden_patterns.message: Leave echo and printf out; one here-document does the whole notice.

test_cases.name: bakery night window
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Dear Harbour Bakery,

We will be doing maintenance on your server during:
    Sunday 02:00-03:00
Your sites may be unavailable for a few minutes.

-- Lanternfish Hosting

test_cases.name: bookshop
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Dear Tidewater Books,

We will be doing maintenance on your server during:
    Wednesday 23:30-23:45
Your sites may be unavailable for a few minutes.

-- Lanternfish Hosting

test_cases.name: awkward characters
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Dear Gull & Anchor Pub,

We will be doing maintenance on your server during:
    Mon 01:00 (UTC)
Your sites may be unavailable for a few minutes.

-- Lanternfish Hosting

title: Color Codes
story:
The big monitor above Mara's desk shows service status as plain white text,
and the harbour-town fog on the windows makes it worse. Ollie suggests
colours: green for good, yellow for trouble, red for disaster. Terminals
have supported that since before Ollie was born; it is done with special
character sequences that start with the Escape character. The service being
checked arrives in the environment as SERVICE.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints three lines, using one printf each:
  <green>OK<reset> <SERVICE> responds in time
  <yellow>WARN<reset> <SERVICE> responds slowly
  <red>FAIL<reset> <SERVICE> does not respond
The colour codes are written \033[32m (green), \033[33m (yellow),
\033[31m (red) and \033[0m (reset). \033 is the Escape character; printf
turns it into the real thing. Only the words OK, WARN and FAIL are coloured:
reset the colour straight after each of them.
concepts: printf translates \033 into the Escape character

required_patterns.message: Use printf; it understands \033 reliably.
Start each coloured word with an escape sequence such as \033[32m.
Reset the colour with \033[0m after each coloured word.

forbidden_patterns.message: Write the escape codes yourself; tput is for another day.

test_cases.name: dory
test_cases.expected_stdout:
[32mOK[0m dory responds in time
[33mWARN[0m dory responds slowly
[31mFAIL[0m dory does not respond

test_cases.name: name with a space
test_cases.expected_stdout:
[32mOK[0m mail relay responds in time
[33mWARN[0m mail relay responds slowly
[31mFAIL[0m mail relay does not respond

test_cases.name: a database
test_cases.expected_stdout:
[32mOK[0m octopus-db responds in time
[33mWARN[0m octopus-db responds slowly
[31mFAIL[0m octopus-db does not respond

title: A Boxed Banner
story:
Gus has discovered that people read a report faster when its title sits in
a box. He wants one for the Monday numbers, and for the week after, and for
the quarterly one, each with a different title (the report tool sets TITLE).
Mara looks at the border of equals signs and says, "Do not type thirty of
those by hand. Teach printf to repeat itself."
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it prints a box 30 characters wide, three lines:
  ==============================
  | <TITLE, padded to 26>      |
  ==============================
The border lines are 30 equals signs. The middle line is "| ", then $TITLE
left-aligned in a 26-character field (%-26s), then " |".
Do not type the equals signs yourself: build the border by repeating one
character 30 times with printf, for example with printf '=%.0s' {1..30}.
concepts: printf reuses its format for every extra argument
%.0s prints nothing but lets the format's own characters repeat

required_patterns.message: Build the box with printf.
Repeat a character to build the border, e.g. printf '=%.0s' {1..30}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not type the border by hand; make printf repeat the character.

title: Status Card
story:
End of week one. Mara asks you for the first real tool of your own: the
status card the team prints for every server. It needs a header for people,
a tidy table of numbers, a note in the log channel about who asked, and an
exit status for the monitoring wall. The collector sets SERVER, UPTIME (days),
ALERTS (open count) and STATUS_CODE (0 fine, 1 warning, 2 critical) before
it calls you. Everything you learned this week is in this one script.
objective:
Write solution.sh. To standard output print, for example with
SERVER=anchovy UPTIME=118 ALERTS=3:
  === STATUS CARD: anchovy ===
  Region: harbour-east
  uptime days    118
  open alerts      3
The first two lines come from one cat <<EOF here-document (with $SERVER
expanded). The two number lines use printf '%-12s %5d\n': the label
left-aligned in 12, the number right-aligned in 5.
To standard error print one line:  <script name>: card printed for <SERVER>
where the script name comes from $(basename "$0").
Finally exit with the status in $STATUS_CODE (exit "$STATUS_CODE").
concepts: exit with a status taken from a variable

required_patterns.message: Print the header with a here-document: cat <<EOF.
Use printf with %-12s for the labels.
Use %5d for the numbers.
Send the log note to stderr with >&2.
Finish with exit "$STATUS_CODE".

test_cases.name: healthy server
test_cases.expected_stdout:
=== STATUS CARD: anchovy ===
Region: harbour-east
uptime days    118
open alerts      3

test_cases.name: warning
test_cases.expected_stdout:
=== STATUS CARD: barracuda ===
Region: harbour-east
uptime days      7
open alerts     21

test_cases.name: critical and fresh
test_cases.expected_stdout:
=== STATUS CARD: sea-urchin-9 ===
Region: harbour-east
uptime days      0
open alerts      0

title: Store a Value
story:
Mara slides the server inventory binder across the desk. It is forty pages of
sticky notes, and Ollie has been retyping "anchovy" at the top of every one.
"Computers are good at remembering things," she says. "Teach this script to
remember the name once, and to remember where the machine is racked."
objective:
Write solution.sh that stores two values in variables and prints them.

  1. Store the text anchovy in a variable called server.
  2. Store the value of the environment setting RACK in a variable called rack
     (the inventory tool passes RACK in, just like $USER and $HOME).
  3. Print exactly two lines, using the variables rather than retyping the values:

       server: anchovy
       rack: <value of RACK>

Remember: no spaces around the = sign when you assign.

required_patterns.message: Assign the server name with server=anchovy (no spaces around =).
Copy the rack into your own variable with rack=$RACK.
Print the server variable with $server instead of typing the name again.
Print the rack variable with $rack.

title: Braces Around Names
story:
Theo's nightly backup produced a folder full of files called just
".tar.gz". Nobody knows which server they came from. He swears the script
said "$NODE_backup.tar.gz" and that Bash must be broken. Mara raises one
eyebrow and tells you to write the naming helper properly.
objective:
The backup tooling passes the server name in the environment setting NODE.
Write solution.sh that prints exactly three lines:

  archive: <NODE>_backup.tar.gz
  replica: <NODE>2
  host: <NODE>.lanternfish.example

For example, with NODE=dory the second line is "replica: dory2".
Use ${NODE} with braces wherever text is glued directly onto the name.
concepts: ${var} braces mark where a name ends

required_patterns.message: Write ${NODE}_backup.tar.gz - without braces Bash looks for a variable called NODE_backup.
Write ${NODE}2 so the 2 is not read as part of the name.

test_cases.expected_stdout:
archive: dory_backup.tar.gz
replica: dory2
host: dory.lanternfish.example

test_cases.name: eel
test_cases.expected_stdout:
archive: eel_backup.tar.gz
replica: eel2
host: eel.lanternfish.example

test_cases.name: name already ends in a digit
test_cases.expected_stdout:
archive: grouper9_backup.tar.gz
replica: grouper92
host: grouper9.lanternfish.example

title: Quote Your Variables
story:
Noor forwards a ticket marked URGENT: the welcome-note script worked for
"Harbour" but fell over on "Gull & Anchor Pub", and for one customer whose
account name is literally "*" it welcomed every file in the folder. Somebody
wrote the script in a hurry and left the variables bare. Mara hands it to
you with a smile.
objective:
solution.sh already contains the hurried (broken) script. Fix it without
changing what it is supposed to do. The customer name arrives in the
environment setting CUSTOMER and may contain spaces, ampersands or a star.

The script must:
  1. Create a file called "<CUSTOMER>.txt" in the current folder containing
     the single line:  Welcome, <CUSTOMER>
  2. Print the line:   Filed: [<CUSTOMER>]

Put every use of the variable inside double quotes.
concepts: "$var" keeps spaces and stars as plain text

required_patterns.message: Put the variable inside double quotes: "$CUSTOMER".

forbidden_patterns.message: A bare $CUSTOMER is still on a line - wrap it in double quotes.

title: Glue Strings Together
story:
Gus wants a clickable link to every status page in the weekly report, and
he wants it by lunch. Each link is the same kind of string with different
pieces: a site, a port and a stage. Rather than typing forty URLs, you will
build one piece at a time, the way Mara builds a sentence she is not sure
about yet.
objective:
The report tool passes in three settings: SITE (a hostname), PORT (a number)
and STAGE (a word such as live or test).

Write solution.sh that builds a variable called url in steps and prints it
as a single line:

  https://<SITE>:<PORT>/status/<STAGE>

Start with url=https://..., then add the remaining pieces to url one by
one with the += operator. Finally print the url.

required_patterns.message: Start the link with url=https://... in your own variable.
Add the remaining pieces with url+=... (append to the variable).

test_cases.name: default https port is still written out

title: Capture Command Output
story:
The inventory file fixtures/servers.txt lists one server per line, in the
order somebody remembered them. Priya needs the alphabetical first and last
names for the audit header. You could copy them by eye, but the list grows
every month, and Mara says people who copy by eye are people who make
mistakes at 2 a.m.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads fixtures/servers.txt (one server name per line)
and prints exactly three lines:

  first: <alphabetically first name>
  last: <alphabetically last name>
  range: <first>..<last>

Capture the first and last name into variables called first and last with
command substitution (first=$(...), last=$(...)), then use only those
variables to print the lines. The file may be replaced by a different list
when your script is checked.

required_patterns.message: Capture the first name with first=$( ... ).
Capture the last name with last=$( ... ).

test_cases.name: the shipped inventory
test_cases.expected_stdout:
first: anchovy
last: marlin
range: anchovy..marlin

test_cases.name: a different list
test_cases.expected_stdout:
first: barracuda
last: halibut
range: barracuda..halibut

test_cases.name: only one server
test_cases.expected_stdout:
first: octopus
last: octopus
range: octopus..octopus

title: Read-Only Settings
story:
Last month a log-cleanup script quietly changed its own retention setting
halfway through and deleted three weeks of Tidewater Books' backups. Priya
does not shout, which is worse. She asks for a setting that, once chosen,
cannot be changed by any line further down the file - and for Bash to
complain loudly the moment somebody tries.
objective:
The config tooling passes two settings: KEEP_DAYS (the retention to apply)
and NEW_DAYS (a "careless" later value that must NOT win).

Write solution.sh that does these things in this order:
  1. Make RETENTION_DAYS a read-only variable holding the value of KEEP_DAYS.
  2. Print:  retention: <RETENTION_DAYS> days
  3. Try to change it with the plain assignment RETENTION_DAYS=$NEW_DAYS.
  4. Print:  retention now: <RETENTION_DAYS> days

Because the variable is read-only, Bash refuses step 3 and prints an error
mentioning "readonly variable" on stderr. The script carries on, and the
value is still the original one, so both lines on stdout show the
KEEP_DAYS value. That is the expected result.
concepts: assignment to a read-only variable is an error

required_patterns.message: Lock the variable with readonly RETENTION_DAYS=...

test_cases.name: the new value is the same as the old one

title: Unset and Check
story:
Priya found an API token sitting in a variable long after the script had
finished using it. "If it is not needed, it should not exist," she says,
and asks for a small audit routine: say whether the token is present
before, wipe it, and prove that it is gone afterwards. Ollie asks what
happens if the token was set to nothing at all. Good question - your
report should tell the difference.
objective:
The vault tooling may or may not pass a setting called TOKEN (it can also
pass it empty). Write solution.sh that prints exactly two lines:

  before=[X]
  after=[Y]

where X is the word set if TOKEN exists (even when its value is empty)
and nothing at all if TOKEN does not exist, and Y is computed the same way
after you remove TOKEN with unset.

Use the ${TOKEN+set} expansion to test existence: it gives the word set
when the variable exists and an empty string when it does not.

required_patterns.message: Test existence with ${TOKEN+set}.
Remove the variable with unset TOKEN.

title: Integer Variables
story:
Gus is pricing next year's harbour-side rack space and needs one number:
how many servers does Lanternfish run? The three team leads each reported
a count, and Ollie's first attempt printed "3+2+1" as the answer. Gus did
not laugh. Teach the variable to do arithmetic.
objective:
The inventory tooling passes three counts as settings: WEB, DB and CACHE
(whole numbers, possibly 0).

Write solution.sh that:
  1. Declares a variable called total as an integer variable.
  2. Sets total to WEB + DB + CACHE and prints:   servers: <total>
  3. Adds 2 spare machines to total with total+=2 and prints:
                                                  with spares: <total>

Example: WEB=3 DB=2 CACHE=1 prints "servers: 6" and "with spares: 8".

required_patterns.message: Mark total as an integer variable with declare -i total.
Add the spares with total+=2 (on an integer variable this adds).

title: Fallback Values
story:
Theo's log viewer works beautifully on his laptop, where he has every
setting exported, and crashes on the support desk machines, where nobody
has set anything. Noor has been phoning him about it. Mara's rule for
tools that other people run: every setting needs a sensible default, so
the tool works the moment it is started.
objective:
The viewer reads three optional settings from the environment: LOG_LEVEL,
LOG_DIR and MAX_LINES. Any of them may be missing or empty.

Write solution.sh that prints exactly three lines:

  level=<LOG_LEVEL, or info when missing or empty>
  dir=<LOG_DIR, or /var/log/lanternfish when missing or empty>
  lines=<MAX_LINES, or 200 when missing or empty>

Use the ${name:-default} form for each of them; do not assign to the
variables and do not use if statements.
concepts: empty counts as missing with the colon

required_patterns.message: Use ${LOG_LEVEL:-info} for the level.
Use ${LOG_DIR:-...} for the directory.
Use ${MAX_LINES:-200} for the line count.

forbidden_patterns.message: No if statements here - the fallback form does the job.

title: Assign a Default
story:
The deploy helper mentions the target region in three different places:
the banner, the backup folder and the tag on the release. Last Tuesday
someone forgot to set REGION, and the banner said "north-pier" (from a
default) while the backup folder was called "/backups/" with nothing after
it. Mara frowns at the diff. "Decide the default once," she says. "Then
everything agrees."
objective:
The deploy tool may pass a setting called REGION (it may be missing or
empty). Write solution.sh that settles REGION once, near the top, with the
default north-pier, and then uses plain $REGION in three lines:

  deploying to <REGION>
  backups: /backups/<REGION>
  tag: release-<REGION>

Use the ${REGION:=north-pier} form so the default is assigned to the
variable. Do not write a separate REGION=... line and do not repeat the
default anywhere else.

required_patterns.message: Settle the default once with ${REGION:=north-pier}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not assign REGION with a separate line; let ${REGION:=...} do it.
Use := (assign) rather than :- (only substitute) so later lines see the value.

title: Fail Loudly When Missing
story:
The nightly database backup ran for two weeks against... nothing. Nobody
had set DB_HOST on the new machine, so the script cheerfully dumped the
database at "" and reported success. North Pier Dental's receptionist found
out when she needed a record from last Thursday. Priya says some settings
have no sensible default, and a script that cannot work should say so and
stop.
objective:
The backup tool passes the database host in the environment setting
DB_HOST. Write solution.sh that:

  1. Prints:  backup job starting
  2. Reads DB_HOST into a variable called host, and if DB_HOST is missing
     or empty stops the script right there with the error message
     "DB_HOST must be set" on stderr and exit status 1. Do this with the
     ${DB_HOST:?message} expansion, not with an if statement.
  3. Otherwise prints:  dumping database on <host>

The error message must contain the text: DB_HOST must be set

required_patterns.message: Use ${DB_HOST:?DB_HOST must be set} for the required setting.

forbidden_patterns.message: No if statement needed - the :? expansion stops the script itself.

dumping database on dory.lanternfish.example

test_cases.name: another host
test_cases.expected_stdout:
backup job starting
dumping database on eel.lanternfish.example

title: Empty Is Not Unset
story:
Noor's ticket form has two optional fields. A customer who leaves the
NOTE field untouched should see "(no note on file)". But a customer who
deliberately clears the note must be left alone - an empty note is a
decision, not an omission. The contact address is the opposite: an empty
address is useless, so it always falls back to the support desk.
One script, two kinds of "missing".
objective:
The ticket tooling passes two settings, NOTE and CONTACT. Either may be
unset, empty, or filled in. Write solution.sh that prints exactly:

  note=[<NOTE>]
  contact=[<CONTACT>]

Rules:
  - NOTE falls back to "(no note on file)" only when NOTE is completely
    unset. An empty NOTE stays empty. Use ${NOTE-...} (no colon).
  - CONTACT falls back to "support@lanternfish.example" when it is unset
    OR empty. Use ${CONTACT:-...} (with a colon).

required_patterns.message: NOTE needs the no-colon form ${NOTE-...}: only an unset NOTE gets the fallback.
CONTACT needs the colon form ${CONTACT:-...}: empty counts as missing.

test_cases.name: note cleared on purpose, contact given

title: Exported to Children
story:
Theo wrote a reporting tool (fixtures/child.sh) that prints the region it
was started for. He swears it prints an empty region "only when you run
it from your script". Priya's reaction: "Of course. It is a different
program. It sees what you hand to it, not everything you keep in your
pockets." She also insists the scratch folder path stays private to your
script, because the tool has no business knowing it.
objective:
The scheduler passes a setting called SITE (the site name, may contain
spaces). Write solution.sh that:

  1. Sets a variable REGION to the value of SITE, in a way that makes it
     visible to programs your script starts.
  2. Sets a variable SCRATCH to /srv/scratch/<SITE>. This one must stay
     private: do NOT export it.
  3. Runs the reporting tool:  bash fixtures/child.sh
  4. Then prints:  parent sees: REGION=[<REGION>] SCRATCH=[<SCRATCH>]

Expected output for SITE=north-pier:

  child sees: REGION=[north-pier] SCRATCH=[]
  parent sees: REGION=[north-pier] SCRATCH=[/srv/scratch/north-pier]
concepts: export makes a variable visible to child processes
unexported variables stay private to the script

required_patterns.message: Make REGION visible to the child with export.

forbidden_patterns.message: SCRATCH must stay private - do not export it.

title: Environment Overrides
story:
Lanternfish's web app runs in three places: Theo's laptop, the staging
box, and production. Each needs a slightly different port and worker count,
and nobody wants to edit the script to change them. The hosting platform
sets a generic PORT; a deployer may override it with the more specific
APP_PORT; and when neither is there the app needs to start anyway.
Mara calls this "layered settings", and says it is half of what makes a
script pleasant to operate.
objective:
Write solution.sh that works out the app's settings from the environment
and prints this exact block (one setting per line):

  name=<APP_NAME, default lanternfish-web>
  mode=<APP_MODE, default production>
  port=<APP_PORT; if that is missing or empty then PORT; if that is also
        missing or empty then 8080>
  workers=<APP_WORKERS, default 2>
  listen=<name>:<port>

"Missing or empty" counts the same everywhere. Compute each setting once
into a variable (name, mode, port, workers), then print using the
variables. For the port, nest one fallback inside another.
concepts: settings from the environment with fallbacks

required_patterns.message: Chain the fallbacks for the port: ${APP_PORT:-${PORT:-8080}}.
Read the other settings into variables with ${APP_NAME:-...} and friends.

title: Swap Two Values
story:
The primary database server at Lanternfish has a hiccup, and the standby
must take over. The failover checklist begins with "swap the roles", and
Ollie, trying to be helpful, wrote PRIMARY=$STANDBY and then STANDBY=$PRIMARY
- and ended up with two servers both called the same thing. Mara slides a
coffee mug across the desk and says: "Think of two glasses of juice. You
need a third glass."
objective:
The failover tooling passes the current roles in the environment settings
PRIMARY and STANDBY (each is one server name, possibly with spaces).

Write solution.sh that:
  1. Prints:  before: primary=<PRIMARY> standby=<STANDBY>
  2. Swaps the two values so that PRIMARY holds what STANDBY held and
     STANDBY holds what PRIMARY held. Do this by assigning to the two
     variables themselves, using a temporary third variable.
  3. Prints:  after: primary=<PRIMARY> standby=<STANDBY>

required_patterns.message: Assign to PRIMARY itself - the swap must change the variables.
Assign to STANDBY itself - the swap must change the variables.

before: primary=dory standby=eel
after: primary=eel standby=dory

after: primary=new eel standby=old dory

after: primary= standby=halibut

title: Indirect References
story:
Gus keeps each customer's storage quota as a separate setting named after
them: LIMIT_bakery, LIMIT_books, LIMIT_dental, and so on. Noor needs a tiny
tool that answers "what is the quota for this customer?" for whichever name
the desk types in. The variable's name is not known until the script runs.
Ollie asks if you have to write a case statement for every customer. You
do not.
objective:
The desk tool passes the customer's short name in the environment setting
CUSTOMER, next to the quota settings (LIMIT_bakery=50, LIMIT_books=120, ...).
The quota for a customer lives in the variable named LIMIT_ followed by the
customer's short name.

Write solution.sh that builds that variable name in a variable called
quota_var, looks up the value of the variable it names, and prints:

  quota for <CUSTOMER>: <value>

If that quota variable does not exist or is empty, print "unlimited" in
place of the value. Use the ${!quota_var} indirect expansion.
concepts: building a variable name at run time

required_patterns.message: Look the value up indirectly with ${!quota_var}.
Build the variable name with quota_var=LIMIT_$CUSTOMER (or similar).

title: The Last Exit Status
story:
Before a server gets a new customer, Mara wants to know whether it is still
in service or has been retired to the lobster-pot graveyard. The inventory
keeps two plain lists, fixtures/active.txt and fixtures/retired.txt, one
name per line. Every command Bash runs leaves behind a number saying how it
went, and that number disappears the moment the next command runs. Your
job is to catch both numbers before they vanish.
objective:
The inventory tool passes the server name in the setting HOST. Write
solution.sh that checks the two lists with grep, using grep -q -x -F so
that only a whole-line match counts and nothing is printed:

  grep -q -x -F "$HOST" fixtures/active.txt
  grep -q -x -F "$HOST" fixtures/retired.txt

Immediately after each grep, copy the special variable $? into a variable
(active_rc and retired_rc). Then print:

  active=<active_rc>
  retired=<retired_rc>

and finally end the script with the same exit status as the first check
(exit "$active_rc"). grep returns 0 when it finds the line and 1 when it
does not.

required_patterns.message: Save the status right after the first grep with active_rc=$?.
Save the status right after the second grep with retired_rc=$?.

title: Server Profile Card
story:
End of week one. Mara hands you a printed copy of the first server card
you made on Monday: it is full of hand-typed values and one of them is
already wrong. "Make the card a script," she says. "Give it a server name
and it fills in everything else, sensible defaults and all. Show me you
learned something this week." Gus wants one for every machine by Friday.
objective:
The card tool passes settings in the environment: SERVER (required),
ROLE (optional, default web), RAM_GB (optional, default 8) and DIMMS
(optional, default 2). The file fixtures/owners.txt has lines like
"dory:Tidewater Books" (server, colon, customer).

Write solution.sh that:
  - Stops with "SERVER must be set" on stderr and exit status 1 if SERVER
    is missing or empty (before printing anything), using ${SERVER:?...}.
  - Locks the company name in a read-only variable:
    readonly COMPANY="Lanternfish Hosting".
  - Uses defaults for ROLE, RAM_GB and DIMMS with ${...:-...}.
  - Declares an integer variable per_dimm with declare -i and sets it to
    RAM_GB divided by DIMMS (whole-number division).
  - Captures the owner with owner=$(...) by searching fixtures/owners.txt
    for the line starting with "<SERVER>:" and cutting out the part after
    the colon. If there is no such line, the owner is "unassigned".
  - Prints exactly this card (a here-document is a good fit):

      === Lanternfish Hosting ===
      server: <SERVER>
      role:   <ROLE>
      memory: <RAM_GB> GB (<DIMMS> x <per_dimm> GB)
      owner:  <owner>
      slug:   <SERVER>_<ROLE>
concepts: defaults, required settings, integers, readonly and captured output together

required_patterns.message: Require SERVER with ${SERVER:?SERVER must be set}.
Lock the company name with readonly COMPANY=...
Give ROLE its default with ${ROLE:-web}.
Declare per_dimm as an integer with declare -i.
Capture the owner from fixtures/owners.txt with owner=$(...).
Build the slug with braces around both names, e.g. ${server}_${role}.

memory: 8 GB (2 x 4 GB)
owner:  Harbour Bakery
slug:   anchovy_web

server: kraken

memory: 10 GB (4 x 2 GB)
owner:  unassigned
slug:   kraken_web

server: eel

memory: 8 GB (2 x 4 GB)
owner:  Gull & Anchor Pub
slug:   eel_cache

title: First Argument
story:
Until today your scripts talked to nobody. Then Noor walked over with a sticky
note: every time a new customer signs up, she types their name into a welcome
message by hand, and last week "Tidewater Books" became "Tidewater Boks".
She wants a script she can hand the name to once.
objective:
Write solution.sh so that it takes ONE argument, the customer name, and prints
exactly one line:
  Ahoy, <name>! Your Lanternfish account is ready.
The name may contain spaces when the caller quotes it, for example
./solution.sh "Tidewater Books" must print:
  Ahoy, Tidewater Books! Your Lanternfish account is ready.

title: Several Arguments
story:
Gus is building the monthly report and needs one line per customer: who they
are, which plan they are on and how many seats they pay for. The sales sheet
gives him those three facts in that order, and he would rather paste them onto
a command line than retype a sentence forty times.
objective:
Write solution.sh taking three arguments in this order: CUSTOMER, PLAN, SEATS.
Print exactly one line:
  <CUSTOMER> -> <SEATS> seats on the <PLAN> plan
Example: ./solution.sh "North Pier Dental" harbour 12 prints
  North Pier Dental -> 12 seats on the harbour plan

required_patterns.message: Use $2 as well: each argument has its own number.
The seat count is the third argument, $3.

test_cases.expected_stdout: Dory -> 1 seats on the starter plan

test_cases.expected_stdout: Gull & Anchor Pub -> 250 seats on the deepwater plan

title: Counting Arguments
story:
Priya is planning the Friday patch window. The wrapper she runs takes a list of
servers as arguments, and last month someone passed thirty and nobody noticed
until the load graphs went red. She wants a quick gate that says how big the
batch is before anything touches a machine.
objective:
Write solution.sh that accepts any number of server names as arguments
(including none) and prints exactly one line:
  batch size: <N>
where N is how many arguments were passed. A name containing spaces, passed in
quotes, counts as one argument.

required_patterns.message: Ask Bash for the argument count with $#.

title: Keep Arguments Intact
story:
Theo wrote a wrapper around the label printer in fixtures/tag.sh. Customers like
"Tidewater Books" keep coming out of the printer as two labels, "Tidewater" and
"Books", and one empty customer vanished entirely. Theo swears the printer is
fine. He is right, and the bug is in how his wrapper passes things along.
objective:
Write solution.sh as a wrapper: it must call the label printer and hand it
every argument it received, unchanged, in the same order.
The printer is run as
  bash fixtures/tag.sh ARGUMENTS...
and prints one line per argument it got, as <argument>. Your wrapper prints
whatever the printer prints, nothing more. An argument with spaces must stay one
label, and an empty argument ("") must stay one empty label: <>.
concepts: "$@" keeps every argument as its own word

required_patterns.message: Pass the arguments on with the quoted form "$@".

forbidden_patterns.message: An unquoted $@ (or $*) splits arguments on spaces. Use "$@".

title: Join Arguments
story:
Ollie is writing the maintenance banner for the status page and needs the
affected servers in a single comma-separated line: "eel,flounder,grouper". He
tried a loop with a trailing comma problem, and a comma at the very end of the
banner ended up in front of customers. There is a built-in way to join words
that never leaves a stray separator.

Write solution.sh that takes any number of server names as arguments and prints
one line:
  affected: <names joined with commas, no spaces>
Example: ./solution.sh eel flounder grouper prints
  affected: eel,flounder,grouper
With one argument there is no comma. A name with spaces inside stays intact.
Do not use a loop, tr, sed or paste.

the first character of IFS is the glue

Set IFS to the character that should glue the words together.

spaces inside a name are kept

title: Walk with shift
story:
Mara's rollout tool is called like this: the first word is the environment, and
everything after it is a server to roll out to. Her old script kept dragging
"$1" into the middle of the server list. She asks you for a version that
takes the environment off the front and leaves only the servers behind.

Write solution.sh. Its first argument is an environment name, the remaining
arguments are servers. Print exactly two lines:
  environment: <first argument>
  targets=<N> [<servers separated by single spaces>]
where N is the number of servers (arguments after the first). With no servers,
the second line is  targets=0 []
You may assume at least the environment is given. Use shift to remove the
environment from the argument list.
concepts: shift drops $1 and renumbers the rest

required_patterns.message: Use shift to remove the environment from the front of the list.

test_cases.name: a server with a space stays one target

title: Require an Argument
story:
Noor's lookup tool is called with a customer name. Yesterday the junior desk
ran it with nothing at all, it printed "Looking up customer: " and happily
carried on to the billing database with a blank name. Priya would like scripts
that refuse to start when their input is missing, and that say how to be used.
objective:
Write solution.sh that needs exactly one argument, the customer name.
- With an argument: print  Looking up customer: <name>  to stdout and exit 0.
- With no arguments: print nothing to stdout, print
    usage: solution.sh CUSTOMER
  to stderr and exit with status 2.
Exit status 2 is the convention for "the command was used wrongly".
Hint for the check, since if/else comes later: this one-liner is enough:
  [[ $# -lt 1 ]] && { echo "message" >&2; exit 2; }

The usage message belongs on stderr: add >&2 to the echo.
Leave with exit 2 so callers can tell it was a usage error.

title: Optional Second Argument

Almost every Lanternfish server listens for remote logins on port 22, so typing
it every time is noise. Theo's connect helper should take just the hostname in
the normal case, and still let him name a port for the odd box that is
different, like the old backup server behind the harbour firewall.

Write solution.sh taking HOST (required) and PORT (optional). Print one line:
  connect <HOST> on port <PORT>
When PORT is not given, or is given as an empty string (""), use 22.
You may assume HOST is always supplied. Use the ${name:-default} expansion,
not a separate check.

title: Read a Line
story:
The support desk pipes ticket titles into a pager script straight from the
ticketing system: one title arrives on standard input, and nobody types it as an
argument. Some titles contain Windows paths such as C:\backups\nightly, and the
last pager mangled every backslash into thin air, which made the on-call engineer
hunt for a folder that does not exist.

Write solution.sh that reads ONE line from standard input into a variable and
prints:
  paging on-call about: <the line>
The line must come out exactly as it went in, including any backslashes.

title: Prompt on stderr
story:
Ollie tried the restart helper for the first time and stared at a blinking cursor
for a full minute: nothing told him that the script was waiting for a server
name. Mara wants a friendly question to appear when a human runs it, but she also
uses the helper in pipelines, where the question must never end up mixed into
the program's real output.
objective:
Write solution.sh that asks "Server to restart: " using read's built-in prompt
option, reads the answer, and prints exactly one line to stdout:
  restart queued for <answer>
The prompt itself must not appear on stdout. (Bash shows read -p prompts on
stderr, and only when input comes from a terminal; in the tests stdin is a pipe,
so stderr must stay empty.)
concepts: the prompt goes to stderr, not stdout

required_patterns.message: Use read -p (for example read -rp "Server to restart: " name).

title: Read Several Fields
story:
The asset inventory is a text file where each line says "hostname address role",
separated by spaces. Gus wants a tidier card for each one on his report, with the
role first because that is how he thinks about the fleet. Some roles are two
words, like "web frontend", and the card must not lose the second word.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads ONE line from stdin with a single read command into
three variables: host, address and role. Print:
  role=<role> host=<host> address=<address>
The first word is the host, the second is the address, and everything left on
the line (even several words) is the role. If the line has only two words, the
role is empty and the output ends with  role= host=...  as usual.
concepts: read -r a b c splits a line into fields
the last variable collects the rest of the line

required_patterns.message: Give read three variable names: read -r host address role.

title: Read into an Array
story:
Customers can tag their servers with labels, and the tags arrive as one
comma-separated line, for example "web,eu-west,critical". They can have any
number of tags. Noor's dashboard wants a summary: how many tags, the first one
and the last one, because those are the ones that decide who gets woken up.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads one line from stdin containing tags separated by
commas (no spaces around the commas) and stores them in an ARRAY with a single
read command. Print exactly:
  count=<number of tags> first=<first tag> last=<last tag>
Example: input  web,eu-west,critical  gives
  count=3 first=web last=critical
The input always has at least one tag.
concepts: read -ra stores the fields in an array

required_patterns.message: Read the line into an array with read -ra NAME.

test_cases.name: tags with a dash and digits

title: Secret Input
story:
Priya reviewed Theo's database-reset helper and went quiet in the way that means
trouble: it asked for the admin password with a plain read, so every character
appeared on the terminal, in screen shares and in the shell logs of the
recording tool. Her rule is simple: a secret is never shown and never printed
back, not even "to confirm".
objective:
Write solution.sh that asks for a password on stdin WITHOUT echoing it to the
terminal, using read's silent option, then prints exactly one line:
  password stored (<N> characters)
where N is the length of what was typed. The password itself must never be
printed to stdout or stderr. After a silent read the cursor stays on the same
line, so also print an empty line to stderr (echo >&2) to finish the line.
concepts: ${#var} is the length of a value

required_patterns.message: Read the password silently with read -s (for example read -rsp ...).

title: Is It a Number?
story:
The disk-quota tool takes a size in gigabytes. A customer once typed "5O" with a
capital letter O instead of a zero, and the tool cheerfully set their quota to
something else entirely. Theo wants the tool to look at the value before doing
anything with it, and to say clearly what it did not like.
objective:
Write solution.sh taking one argument, QUOTA. A valid quota is a whole number
made only of digits 0-9 (no sign, no decimal point, no spaces).
- Valid: print  quota set to <QUOTA> GB  and exit 0.
- Invalid: print nothing to stdout, print
    error: not a whole number: <QUOTA>
  to stderr and exit 1.
Check with a regular-expression test inside [[ ]], not with an external tool.
You may assume exactly one argument is passed.

required_patterns.message: Match the value against a pattern with [[ $quota =~ ... ]].
The pattern should describe digits, for example ^[0-9]+$.

title: Reject Empty Input
story:
The billing import asks the desk for a customer code on each run. Last Friday
someone just hit Enter, the script carried on with an empty code, and the
invoice went out addressed to nobody. Gus is not amused; Mara wants an empty
answer to be refused, the same way whether the person pressed Enter or the
input ended without any line at all.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads one line from stdin into a variable called code.
- If the line is empty, or there is no input at all (end of file), print nothing
  to stdout, print  error: customer code is empty  to stderr and exit 1.
- Otherwise print  code accepted: <code>  and exit 0.
Use the -z test for emptiness. Codes with spaces inside, such as "NP D 7", are
accepted as typed.
Careful: when stdin has no line, read returns a failure status, and under
set -e that would end the script silently. Make the read tolerant with || true.
concepts: [[ -z $var ]] is true when the value is empty
read at end of file fails; || true keeps set -e calm

required_patterns.message: Test for emptiness with [[ -z $code ]].
End the read with || true so a missing line does not stop the script under set -e.

title: Arguments or stdin
story:
Ollie asks a good question: "Why can I type ./check.sh anchovy but not pipe
the hostname in?" Good Unix tools do both. Theo's health-check script should
take the hostname as an argument when one is given, and otherwise read it from
standard input, so it works in a terminal, in a pipeline and in cron.
objective:
Write solution.sh that finds a hostname like this:
  1. If an argument is given, use the first argument (ignore stdin).
  2. Otherwise read one line from stdin.
Print  checking <hostname>  and exit 0.
If there is no argument and stdin gives no usable line (empty line or no input),
print  usage: solution.sh [HOSTNAME]  to stderr, nothing to stdout, and exit 2.
concepts: fall back to stdin when no arguments are given
${1:-} as a safe way to look at an optional argument

required_patterns.message: When there is no argument, read the hostname from stdin.
Use ${1:-} to look at the first argument safely, even when it is missing.

test_cases.name: blank stdin line is not a hostname

title: Read Until the End
story:
Gus pastes the month's hardware expenses into a terminal, one per line, as
"item cost", for example "usb-cable 12". He has never once pasted the same
number of lines, so a script that reads exactly three lines is no use. He wants
it to keep going until the paste ends and then give him the totals, which he
will copy straight into the board report.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads lines from stdin until the input ends. Each line is
an item name and a whole-number cost separated by whitespace, for example
"usb-cable 12". Print one final line:
  items=<number of lines> total=<sum of all costs>
With empty input print  items=0 total=0
The last line of input may be missing its trailing newline; it must still be
counted. Use a while loop around read.
concepts: while read -r ...; do ...; done loops until EOF
variables built up inside the loop

required_patterns.message: Loop with while read -r ... until the input is exhausted.

test_cases.name: many lines
test_cases.stdin:
a 1
b 2
c 3
d 4
e 5
f 6
g 7
h 8

title: Long Flags by Hand
story:
Noor's new-customer tool grew from one argument to five, and nobody remembers the
order any more: was it name, then plan, then dry-run? Theo proposes named flags,
like the big tools use: --customer "Tidewater Books" --plan harbour. They can
come in any order, and some are optional. You will parse them by hand, the way
scripts did before getopts.
objective:
Write solution.sh accepting these flags in any order:
  --customer NAME   (required, takes a value)
  --plan NAME       (optional, takes a value, default: basic)
  --dry-run         (optional switch, no value)
Print exactly one line:
  customer=<NAME> plan=<PLAN> dry_run=<yes|no>
Errors, all with nothing on stdout and exit status 2:
  - an unrecognised argument: stderr  error: unknown option: <argument>
  - no --customer given:       stderr  usage: solution.sh --customer NAME [--plan PLAN] [--dry-run]
Loop over the arguments with while and case, and use shift to move forward.
concepts: shift 2 consumes a flag together with its value

required_patterns.message: Walk through the arguments with a while loop.
Dispatch on the current argument with case ... esac.
Use shift to consume each flag (shift 2 when it has a value).

forbidden_patterns.message: getopts is the next-but-one level; parse by hand here.

title: getopts Basics
story:
Ollie keeps tailing log excerpts into the team chat and always asks "how do I
get just the first few lines?". Mara decides he should have a tiny preview tool,
built the way classic Unix tools are: single-letter options like -n 5 and -v,
which people can even bundle as -vn 5. Bash ships a built-in parser for exactly
this, so there is no need to write the loop by hand.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a mini "head" that copies lines from stdin to stdout.
Options (parse them with getopts):
  -n COUNT   how many lines to show (default 3)
  -v         verbose: first print the line "showing first <COUNT> lines"
Then print the first COUNT lines of stdin (all of them, if there are fewer).
Options may be bundled, so -vn 2 means -v -n 2. You may assume the options are
valid; the next level deals with mistakes.
Use the head command for the copying, for example  head -n "$count".
concepts: $OPTARG holds the value of an option that takes one
a colon after a letter means the option takes a value

required_patterns.message: Parse the options with getopts, for example getopts "vn:" opt.
The value after -n is in $OPTARG.

forbidden_patterns.message: No long options in this level; getopts handles single letters.

title: getopts Error Handling
story:
The port-probe tool you are about to finish will be used by the whole support
desk, and the desk makes typos. Last week "-P 443" produced a cryptic message
from getopts, and "-p" with no number went on to probe port nothing. Mara wants
every user mistake explained in the tool's own words, with a clear exit status
the monitoring scripts can react to.
objective:
Write solution.sh with these options, parsed by getopts in silent error mode
(an option string that starts with a colon):
  -h HOST   required, takes a value
  -p PORT   optional, takes a value, default 443
  -q        optional switch: quiet
Output on success (exit 0):
  normal:  probing <HOST> on port <PORT>
  quiet:   <HOST>:<PORT>
Errors (nothing on stdout, exit status 2), each one line on stderr:
  unknown option, for example -x:     error: unknown option: -x
  option missing its value, e.g. -p:  error: option -p needs a value
  no -h given at all:                 usage: solution.sh -h HOST [-p PORT] [-q]
concepts: leading colon in ":h:p:q" turns on silent error reporting
\? branch for unknown options, : branch for missing values
$OPTARG names the offending option in error branches

required_patterns.message: Start the option string with a colon, e.g. getopts ":h:p:q" opt.
Add a \?) branch in the case for unknown options.
Add a :) branch in the case for options that are missing their value.

test_cases.name: quiet mode, options in another order

title: Your First if
story:
Ollie watched Mara deploy last night and asked why she always pauses before
pressing Enter. "Because it was production," she said. "It should say so
out loud." Today you teach the deploy helper to shout a warning, but only
when the target really is production.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the name of the target environment.
If the argument is exactly `prod`, print this single line:
  CAUTION: production - the two-person rule applies
For any other value (staging, an empty string, anything else) print nothing at all.
Use an `if [[ ... ]]; then ... fi` block.
concepts: a test that is true or false

required_patterns.message: Start with if [[ ... ]]; then and close the block with fi.
Every if needs a closing fi.

test_cases.name: production gets the warning
test_cases.expected_stdout: CAUTION: production - the two-person rule applies

title: if and else
story:
Every morning Noor opens the Harbour Bakery ordering-site log and scans it for
the word ERROR. "Most days it is clean," she sighs, "and I still read three
hundred lines to be sure." Let the script do the reading, and have it answer
either way so Noor never wonders whether it ran.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the path of a log file.
If the file contains the word `ERROR` (capitals, exactly), print:
  needs attention: ERROR found in <file>
Otherwise print:
  clean: no ERROR in <file>
where <file> is the path exactly as given. Always print exactly one of the two lines.
Hint for the condition: `grep -q` searches silently and succeeds when it finds a match,
and `if` can test any command, not only `[[ ]]`.
concepts: if testing a command's exit status

required_patterns.message: This level needs both branches: add an else.

title: The elif Ladder
story:
The uptime monitor at Lanternfish sends one number per check: the HTTP status
code the customer's site answered with. Each code has a different runbook line,
and Theo is tired of looking them up at 3 a.m. Teach the helper to translate
the code into the action a human should take.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: an HTTP status code.
Print exactly one line, depending on the code:
  200  ->  healthy: nothing to do
  301  ->  moved: check the redirect
  404  ->  not found: tell Noor
  503  ->  backend down: page Mara
  anything else  ->  unexpected status <code>: ask Theo
Compare the code as a string. Build the decision with if / elif / else.

required_patterns.message: Use elif for the in-between branches.
End the ladder with an else for unexpected codes.

title: Same String?
story:
Priya audits what is actually running against what the release sheet says
should be running. Last week a server was found on "V2.4.1" while the sheet
said "v2.4.1", and nobody noticed because the humans' eyes skipped the capital.
Computers do not skip. Build the drift checker.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: the EXPECTED release tag and the
RUNNING release tag.
If the two are exactly the same string, print:
  in sync: <tag>
Otherwise print:
  DRIFT: expected <expected> but found <running>
Comparison is literal and case-sensitive. A `*` or a space in a tag is just a
character, never a pattern. Use `==` inside `[[ ]]`.
concepts: quote the right-hand side to compare literally

required_patterns.message: Quote the right-hand side of == ("$var") so it is compared literally, not as a pattern.

test_cases.name: different tag
test_cases.expected_stdout: DRIFT: expected v2.4.1 but found v2.4.2

test_cases.name: case matters
test_cases.expected_stdout: DRIFT: expected v2.4.1 but found V2.4.1

test_cases.name: a star is not a wildcard
a star only equals a star

title: Different String?
story:
The nightly customer report must run on exactly one machine: dory, the quiet
standby. Last Tuesday Theo started it on barracuda, the busiest server in the
fleet, in the middle of the lunch rush. Gus noticed the slow checkout before
anyone noticed the cause. Add a guard to the front of the job.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the name of the host it is running on.
If the host is anything other than exactly `dory`, print this to stderr and
exit with status 1, printing nothing to stdout:
  refusing to run on <host>: this job belongs to dory
If the host is `dory`, print to stdout:
  dory: starting nightly report
Use `!=` for the guard.
concepts: a guard clause that exits early

required_patterns.message: Write the guard with the != operator.

title: Empty or Not
story:
Noor's helpdesk form sends tickets to a tiny script. Twice this week a ticket
arrived with no customer name, so nobody knew whose shop was offline. Notes are
optional, but a name is not. Teach the script to insist on the one and
gracefully handle the other.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a customer name ($1) and an optional note ($2).
If the name is missing or empty, print to stderr
  error: customer name required
and exit with status 2 (print nothing to stdout).
Otherwise print
  ticket for: <name>
and, only when the note is not empty, a second line
  note: <note>
Use `-z` to detect an empty name and `-n` to detect a present note.

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -z ... ]] to detect the empty name.
Use [[ -n ... ]] to detect that a note was given.

test_cases.name: name and note
test_cases.expected_stdout:
ticket for: Harbour Bakery
note: oven controller offline

test_cases.name: empty note is the same as no note

title: Comparing Numbers
story:
Grouper's disk filled up at 4 a.m. and took three customer sites with it.
Mara's post-mortem has one action item: a disk check that talks in levels, not
raw percentages, so that whoever reads the alert knows how worried to be.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the disk usage in percent (a whole
number from 0 to 100). Print exactly one line:
  <n>% used: FULL        if the number is exactly 100
  <n>% used: CRITICAL    if it is 90 or more (but not 100)
  <n>% used: WARNING     if it is 70 or more (but under 90)
  <n>% used: OK          otherwise
Compare with the numeric operators -eq, -ge (and friends) inside [[ ]].
Do not use (( )) in this level; it is the next level's tool.

required_patterns.message: Compare the number with -lt, -le, -gt, -ge, -eq or -ne.

forbidden_patterns.message: Save (( )) for the next level; use [[ ... -ge ... ]] here.

title: Arithmetic Tests
story:
Gus has found a line on the bandwidth invoice that makes him wince: customers
who exceed their monthly transfer quota are billed per extra gigabyte, and
nobody told them how far over they were. He wants one sentence per customer,
with the maths done for him.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two whole numbers: gigabytes USED ($1) and the
QUOTA ($2), both in GB.
If used is greater than quota, print
  over quota: <used> GB used of <quota> GB (+<used minus quota> GB)
Otherwise (equal counts as within quota) print
  within quota: <used> GB used of <quota> GB (<quota minus used> GB left)
Write the decision with double parentheses, `if (( used > quota ))`, and
calculate the difference with `$(( ... ))`.

required_patterns.message: Make the decision with if (( used > quota )); then.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use (( )) with > and < here instead of -gt / -lt.

test_cases.name: exactly at the quota
test_cases.expected_stdout: within quota: 500 GB used of 500 GB (0 GB left)

test_cases.expected_stdout: over quota: 101 GB used of 100 GB (+1 GB)

title: Both Must Be True
story:
Priya has finally written down the VPN policy on one line of a whiteboard:
"Staff only, and only with a second factor." Ollie asked what happens to a
contractor with MFA, or a staffer without it. "Both rules must pass, Ollie,"
said Priya. "Not one. Both." Make the access script obey the whiteboard.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: a user name, a group, and an MFA
flag (`yes` or `no`).
Access is granted only when the group is exactly `staff` AND the MFA flag is
exactly `yes`. Print
  granted: <user>
when access is granted and
  denied: <user>
in every other case. Combine both checks into a single condition with `&&`.

required_patterns.message: Combine the two checks with &&.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use one if with && instead of nesting two ifs.

test_cases.name: mfa flag must be exactly yes

title: Either Will Do
story:
The Lanternfish on-call calendar has two rotas: weekdays, where Theo carries
the pager, and "weekend rota", where Mara does. Weekend rota also applies on
public holidays, because the harbour festival does not care what day of the
week it is. Whoever is looking at the clock at 6 a.m. needs the script to say
which rota is in force.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a day (`mon` `tue` `wed` `thu`
`fri` `sat` `sun`, always lowercase) and a holiday flag (`yes` or `no`).
The weekend rota applies if the day is `sat` OR the day is `sun` OR the holiday
flag is `yes`. Print
  weekend rota: Mara has the pager
in that case, otherwise
  weekday rota: Theo has the pager
Put all three checks into one condition joined by `||`.
concepts: any one true condition is enough

required_patterns.message: Join the checks with || ("or").

forbidden_patterns.message: Use || in a single if for this level; case comes later.

title: Flip a Condition
story:
The staging firewall has an allowlist: one IP address per line in a file called
allowlist.txt. Priya's rule is the inverse of what you would think. She does not
care who is on the list; she cares who is not, because those get blocked and
those are the ones that wake her up. Write the check from her point of view.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: an IP address. The file
`allowlist.txt` (in the current directory) lists the allowed addresses, one
per line.
If the address is NOT listed, print
  BLOCK <ip>
If it is listed, print
  allow <ip>
The address must match a whole line exactly, and the dots are ordinary
characters (10.0.0.1 is not 10.0.0.15, and not 10x0x0x1).
Build the decision around `!` (not).

required_patterns.message: Use ! to negate the test, e.g. if ! grep ...; then (or [[ ! ... ]]).

title: Does It Exist?
story:
Ollie wrote a cleanup script last week and pointed it at a path that did not
exist. It deleted nothing and printed nothing, and Ollie declared it a success.
Mara's lesson: a script should look before it leaps. Write the little
inspector every cleanup job should call first.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a path. Print exactly one line,
in the format `<path>: <kind>`, where kind is:
  regular file     if the path is a regular file
  directory        if the path is a directory
  something else   if it exists but is neither (a device, for example)
  not found        if nothing exists at that path
Use the file tests -f, -d and -e, and quote the path (it may contain spaces).

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -f ... ]] to recognise a regular file.
Use [[ -d ... ]] to recognise a directory.
Use [[ -e ... ]] to detect that something exists.

title: Permission Checks
story:
A deploy failed at midnight because someone copied a script to the server and
forgot to make it executable. Priya wants a pre-flight tool that tells you
what YOU, the user running it, can do with a file, in the same compact style
as `ls -l` does: three characters, one per right.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a path.
If nothing exists at the path, print to stderr
  no such file: <path>
and exit with status 1.
Otherwise print `<path>: ` followed by three characters describing what the
current user can do:
  r or -   (can read?)     w or -   (can write?)     x or -   (can execute?)
For example `deploy.sh: rwx` or `notes.txt: rw-` or `locked.key: ---`.
Test with -r, -w and -x (not by parsing ls).

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -r ... ]] to test readability.
Use [[ -w ... ]] to test writability.
Use [[ -x ... ]] to test executability.

forbidden_patterns.message: Test the rights with -r -w -x instead of parsing ls.

title: Empty File?
story:
Gus gets a revenue CSV mailed to him at 6 a.m. every day. On Monday the mail
arrived on time with a perfectly polite attachment of zero bytes. Nobody
noticed until Gus tried to read it in a meeting. Insert a checkpoint before the
mail is sent: an empty report must stop the pipeline.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the path of a report file.
If the file exists and has any content (size greater than zero), print
  ok: <file>, lines: <n>
where <n> is the number of lines in the file.
If the file is empty or does not exist, print to stderr
  empty or missing: <file>
and exit with status 1, printing nothing to stdout.
Use `-s` for the check. (Tip: the line count is `wc -l < "$file"`; wrap it
in `$(( ... ))` or the output may contain extra spaces on macOS.)
concepts: -s true when the file has a size greater than zero

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -s "$file" ]]: true when the file exists and is not empty.

test_cases.name: a blank line is still content

title: Which File Is Newer?
story:
Every night a job copies the customer database dump to the backup folder, and
every morning Mara wonders whether that copy is still from last night or from
last month. "Don't tell me it ran," she says. "Tell me whether the backup is
older than the thing it is supposed to protect." Time to compare two
timestamps.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a SOURCE file and a BACKUP file.
Print
  STALE: <backup> is older than <source>
if the backup does not exist or its modification time is older than the
source's. Otherwise (same age or newer) print
  fresh: <backup> is up to date
Use `-nt` (newer than) or `-ot` (older than) in `[[ ]]`.

required_patterns.message: Compare modification times with [[ a -nt b ]] or [[ a -ot b ]].

test_cases.name: backup is newer
test_cases.expected_stdout: fresh: backup/customers.sql is up to date

test_cases.name: same timestamp counts as fresh
test_cases.expected_stdout: fresh: orders.bak is up to date

test_cases.name: backup never made
test_cases.expected_stdout: STALE: orders.bak is older than orders.sql

title: Glob Matching in [[ ]]
story:
The /var/spool folder on eel is a junk drawer: temp files nobody removed, logs
that should be archived, and crash dumps that Theo wants attached to tickets.
Ollie has a list of file names and no idea what to do with each. Teach the
script the naming conventions so it can sort the drawer one name at a time.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a file name (not a path to check,
just the name). Print `<name> -> <action>` where the action is chosen by the
FIRST rule that matches:
  1. name starts with `tmp-`                         -> delete
  2. name ends with `.log`                           -> archive
  3. name is `crash-`, one single character, `.dump`  -> ticket
  4. anything else                                   -> ignore
Use wildcard patterns on the right-hand side of `==` inside `[[ ]]`; do not
quote the patterns. Do not use `case` (that comes soon).

required_patterns.message: Put an unquoted wildcard pattern (like *.log) on the right of ==.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use if / elif with == patterns in this level.

test_cases.name: rotated log has a different ending

title: case Statements
story:
Lanternfish's in-house service wrapper, `lanternctl`, is mostly a menu: say
"start", "stop", "restart" or "status" and it does the right thing. So far it
is a thicket of elif lines that Mara describes as "a tree I keep walking into".
Rewrite its front end as a tidy command dispatcher.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: an action. Print one line:

After the pager-and-freeze incident, Mara and Priya sit down and write the

not be in a change freeze. Gus asks that it be turned into code before anyone

title: A log() Helper

Marlin's disk-watch script is noisy: when everything is fine it still prints
twelve lines, and when something is wrong the important line is lost among them.

the cron job can stay quiet while a human can turn the noise up.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument PCT (disk usage, a whole number).
Define a function named log that takes a LEVEL word and a message:

important as the threshold in the environment variable LOG_LEVEL
(default INFO). Importance order, lowest first: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.

    log INFO  "checking disk usage"

Friday afternoon, and Mara hands you the last job of the month: the new-customer
provisioning script. It has to take a business name and a disk quota, refuse nonsense,
