prints the decoded token: the same characters in the opposite order. Spaces
and punctuation are characters like any other, and an empty argument prints
an empty line.

  ./solution.sh 321cba      prints  abc123

Build the result with a loop over the character positions (C-style for loop
and ${var:index:1}). Do not use rev, tac, awk, sed or tr.
concepts: ${var:i:1} is the character at position i
a C-style for loop can count downwards

required_patterns.message: Take one character at position i with ${token:i:1}.
Walk the positions with a C-style loop: for (( i = ...; ...; i-- )).

forbidden_patterns.message: Reverse the string with a loop in Bash, not with rev, tac, awk, sed or tr.

title: Regex Match
story:
Release day at Lanternfish. The deploy tool accepts only tags that look like
versions: three numbers separated by dots, with an optional leading "v".
Theo's pipeline keeps shipping oddities like "1.4", "1.4.2-rc1" and "v1.x.0"
and the deploy fails halfway through. Mara asks for a gatekeeper that checks
the shape of a tag before the pipeline goes anywhere near the servers.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads release tags from standard input, one per line.
For each tag print

  <tag>: valid       or       <tag>: invalid

A valid tag is an optional "v", then MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where each part is one or
more digits, and NOTHING else before or after. So v2.0.10 and 1.4.2 are valid;
1.4, 1.4.2-rc1, v1.x.0, 01.2 3.4 and an empty line are not. Test the tag
with the regex operator [[ $tag =~ regex ]], anchored at both ends. No grep, expr,
sed or awk.
concepts: [[ $s =~ regex ]] matches an extended regular expression
^ and $ anchor the regex to both ends

required_patterns.message: Test the tag with [[ $tag =~ regex ]].
Anchor the regex with ^ at the start and $ at the end, or "1.4.2-rc1" would pass.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use [[ $tag =~ regex ]] instead of an external tool.

test_cases.name: empty line and a double v

title: Capture Groups
story:
The reverse proxy in front of every Lanternfish site writes one access-log line
per request, and Gus wants a tidy digest for the quarterly report: which
method, which URL and what status each visitor got. Checking that a line looks
right is not enough this time; the digest needs the pieces. The log also holds
noise lines from other tools that must be reported and skipped, not crash the
script.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads access-log lines from standard input. A request
line looks like
  203.0.113.7 - [07/Nov/2024:09:30:15] "GET /shop/cart HTTP/1.1" 502 1432
i.e. a quoted request "METHOD PATH HTTP/x.y", followed by a 3-digit status.
For each line that matches, print

  <status> <METHOD> <PATH>

(for the example: 502 GET /shop/cart). For each line that does not match, print
"skipped: <the line>". Extract the pieces with capture groups in a [[ =~ ]]
test and read them from the BASH_REMATCH array. No grep, sed or awk.
concepts: ( ) in a regex captures a group
${BASH_REMATCH[1]} is the first group; [0] is the whole match

required_patterns.message: Match each line with [[ $line =~ regex ]].
Read the captured pieces from ${BASH_REMATCH[1]}, ${BASH_REMATCH[2]}, ...

forbidden_patterns.message: Use capture groups with =~ and BASH_REMATCH instead of an external tool.

title: Add Two Numbers
story:
It is capacity planning day, and Gus has cleared his whole calendar for it.
He is standing at your desk with a coffee and a single question: "How much
bandwidth did anchovy and barracuda use between them this month?" Both
servers report a plain number of gigabytes. Time to let Bash do the sums.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two whole numbers as arguments: the gigabytes
used by anchovy ($1) and by barracuda ($2). Print one line:

  combined: <sum> GB

The numbers may be zero, negative (a refund adjustment) or very large.
Use arithmetic expansion, $(( ... )), to add them. Do not use expr or bc.

required_patterns.message: Do the addition inside $(( ... )) arithmetic expansion.

forbidden_patterns.message: Leave expr and bc alone: Bash can add on its own with $(( ... )).

title: Operator Precedence
story:
Gus built the bandwidth invoice in a spreadsheet and the total came out
wildly too high. Theo glances over his shoulder: "You added the base fee to
the gigabytes before multiplying by the rate, didn't you?" Gus did. Bash has
the same rules of precedence as the spreadsheet, so your script had better
get them right the first time.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes four whole numbers:
  $1  SERVERS  number of servers on the plan
  $2  BASE     flat monthly fee per server
  $3  GB       gigabytes of traffic per server
  $4  RATE     price per gigabyte

Print exactly two lines:
  per_server=<BASE + GB * RATE>
  total=<(BASE + GB * RATE) * SERVERS>

Use $(( ... )) and write the expression the way it reads in maths:
multiplication happens before addition, and you need parentheses where the
addition has to happen first.

required_patterns.message: The total needs parentheses inside $(( )): (fee + traffic) * servers.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use $(( )) here, not expr or bc.

title: Division and Remainder
story:
Gus loves the uptime page, but "263520 minutes" means nothing to him. "I need
to know how many days, hours and minutes that is," he says, "so I can write
it in the investor update. Please, in words a person can read." Ollie shyly
adds that he once did this by hand with a calculator and got it wrong twice.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a number of minutes of uptime
(a whole number, zero or more). Print a single line:

  uptime: <D>d <H>h <M>m

where D is the number of whole days (1440 minutes each), H the whole hours
left over after the days (0 to 23) and M the minutes left over after that
(0 to 59). Always print all three parts, even when they are zero.

Use / for division and % for the remainder inside $(( ... )).

required_patterns.message: Use / inside $(( )) to divide.
Use % inside $(( )) to get the remainder.

forbidden_patterns.message: Plain integer division and % are all you need here.

test_cases.name: one minute short of a day

title: Powers
story:
Ollie is setting up a private network for the harbour office and has
discovered the slash notation: "/24", "/28", "/30". "How many machines fit in
a /26?" he asks. Priya, passing with a mug, says "Count the host bits and
raise two to that power." Ollie wants a script instead of a lecture.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: an IPv4 prefix length P, a whole
number from 8 to 30. A network with prefix /P has 32 - P host bits.
Print two lines:

  addresses=<2 to the power of (32 - P)>
  hosts=<addresses minus 2>

(two addresses are reserved: the network address and the broadcast address).
Use the ** power operator inside $(( ... )).

required_patterns.message: Raise 2 to the power of the host bits with the ** operator.

forbidden_patterns.message: Bit shifting would skip the lesson: use ** for the power.
Bash can raise to a power on its own: $(( 2 ** n )).

title: Increment and Decrement
story:
The VPN gateway logs one line every time someone connects or disconnects.
Priya wants to know, from last night's log, how many connections there were
in total and how many people were still connected when the log ended. "Please
don't read it by eye," she says. "Last time I did, I lost count around
line 40."
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads the VPN log from standard input, one event per
line. Each line is either "connect <user>" or "disconnect <user>"; ignore any
other line.

Keep two counters:
  total   goes up by one for every connect line
  active  goes up by one for connect, down by one for disconnect

Afterwards print exactly:
  total_connects=<total>
  still_connected=<active>

(active can be negative when the log starts in the middle of a session.)
Use (( x++ )) and (( x-- )) for the counting.

required_patterns.message: Count up with (( counter++ )).
Count down with (( counter-- )).

forbidden_patterns.message: Use ++ and -- instead of adding or subtracting 1 yourself.

title: Compound Assignment
story:
The database volume on dory holds 100 GB and grows by a steady chunk every
month. Gus has a worry, though: what if the new analytics customer makes the
data double every month instead? "Show me both futures side by side,"
he says, "the boring one and the scary one. Month by month. I want to see
where they split."

Write solution.sh that takes three whole numbers:
  $1  START   the current size in GB
  $2  ADD     GB added every month in the steady scenario
  $3  MONTHS  how many months to project (zero or more)

First print the line
  start=<START>
then, for each month from 1 to MONTHS, one line
  month <M>: steady=<size> doubling=<size>
where "steady" has ADD added to it every month and "doubling" is
multiplied by 2 every month, both starting from START.

Update the two sizes in place with the compound operators += and *=.

Grow the doubling size with *=.

title: let and (( ))
story:
Theo left a script behind before going on holiday, and half of it uses a
strange command called "let" while the other half uses double parentheses.
Mara wants you to understand both before touching it. "They do the same
job," she says, "but they behave a little differently when something
evaluates to zero. Let's see if you catch it."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two whole numbers: TOTAL ($1) and USED ($2),
the size and the used space of a volume in GB (TOTAL is never zero).
Print exactly three lines:

  free=<TOTAL - USED>
  used_pct=<USED * 100 / TOTAL, whole number>
  let_status=<exit status of the let command that computed free>

Compute free with the `let` command (quote its expression), and used_pct with
an assignment inside (( ... )). Read the status with $? on the very next
command after let. Do not use set -e: a let (or (( )) ) whose result is zero
reports failure.

required_patterns.message: Calculate free space with the let command.
Calculate used_pct with an assignment inside (( ... )).

forbidden_patterns.message: Use let and (( )), not expr or bc.

test_cases.name: completely full volume makes let report failure

title: Arithmetic Conditions
story:
Marlin's disk filled up at 3 a.m. last Tuesday and nobody knew until a customer
called. Mara has decided that every disk gets a traffic light: green, amber or
red, based on how full it is. "Keep it simple," she says. "Two thresholds,
and no floating point. If you compare it right, you won't even need
to compute a percentage."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: a server NAME ($1), the USED
space ($2) and the TOTAL size ($3), both whole numbers in GB (TOTAL is always
positive). Print one line:

  <NAME>: <STATUS>

where STATUS is
  CRITICAL   when the disk is 90% full or more
  WARNING    when it is 75% full or more (but below 90%)
  OK         otherwise

Decide with `if (( ... ))` / `elif (( ... ))`. Avoid a percentage division:
compare USED * 100 with TOTAL * 90 (and TOTAL * 75) instead.

required_patterns.message: Use if (( ... )) for the comparisons.

forbidden_patterns.message: Inside (( )) you can write >= and < like in maths; no -ge or -lt needed.
No external tools: (( )) can compare numbers by itself.

test_cases.name: odd sizes where integer division would mislead

title: Decimals with awk
story:
Gus does not want to read "104 dollars" on an invoice: customers pay in
dollars and cents, and the rate is 8.5 cents per gigabyte. Ollie tries
$(( 1234.5 * 0.085 )) in the terminal and gets a stern error message.
"Bash only does whole numbers," Mara explains. "For decimals we borrow awk,
which has been doing floating point since 1977."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments:
  $1  GB       traffic in gigabytes (may have decimals)
  $2  RATE     price per gigabyte in dollars (may have decimals)
  $3  SERVERS  number of servers sharing the bill (a positive whole number)

Print two lines, each with exactly two decimals:
  total=$<GB * RATE>
  per_server=$<GB * RATE / SERVERS>

Do the calculation with awk, using
awk -v name=value 'BEGIN { printf "..." }' (no input files needed).
Do not use bc.

required_patterns.message: Use awk for the decimal arithmetic.
Format the amounts with printf "%.2f" so they always show two decimals.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use awk: it exists on every Linux and macOS machine.

title: Percentages Without Floats
story:
The status page for the harbour cluster needs a usage figure with one
decimal, like "37.5%". Gus wants it exact, Priya refuses to ship a script
that depends on awk being installed on the status box, and Theo mutters that
Bash can't do decimals. "It can fake them," Mara says. "Count in tenths of a
percent, then put the point back when you print."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two whole numbers: USED ($1) and TOTAL ($2).
Print one line:

  usage: <percent>%

where percent is USED / TOTAL * 100 with exactly one decimal digit, cut off
(truncated, not rounded). Examples: 1 of 3 is 33.3%, 2 of 3 is 66.6%,
5 of 2000 is 0.2%, 50 of 50 is 100.0%.

If TOTAL is 0, print "total must not be zero" to stderr and exit with
status 2.

Use integer arithmetic only: scale first (USED * 1000 / TOTAL gives tenths
of a percent), then split the result into whole part and decimal digit.
No awk, no bc.
concepts: scale up, divide, split with / and %

required_patterns.message: Do the scaled division inside $(( )) with /.
Split the tenths into whole and decimal part with % (and /).

forbidden_patterns.message: This level is about doing it with integers only.

test_cases.name: below one percent keeps the leading zero

title: Number Bases
story:
Priya is auditing the firewall. The rule file lists ports in hexadecimal
("1f90") and file modes in octal ("640"), while the dashboard shows decimal.
She keeps converting in her head and keeps losing. "I need a quick table I can
trust," she says. "Port and permission, in the other bases too."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a PORT written in hexadecimal
($1, digits 0-9 and a-f or A-F, no 0x prefix) and a MODE written in octal
($2, digits 0-7, possibly with a leading zero like 0644).
Print exactly four lines:

  port=<PORT in decimal>
  mode=<MODE in decimal>
  port_octal=<the port in octal>
  mode_hex=<the mode in lowercase hexadecimal>

Read the numbers with Bash's base#number notation inside $(( )), and write
the other bases with printf (%o and %x). No bc, no awk.

required_patterns.message: Read the hex port with 16#<digits> inside $(( )).
Read the octal mode with 8#<digits> inside $(( )).
Write numbers in other bases with printf %o or %x.

forbidden_patterns.message: Bash can read any base itself with base#number.

single byte and a leading-zero mode
leading zeros on the hex port

title: Random in a Range
story:
Every customer's nightly backup used to start at exactly 02:00, and at
02:00 exactly the whole harbour network ground to a halt. Mara's fix is
"jitter": every job waits a random number of minutes before it begins, so the
load spreads out. She needs a small generator that picks those delays from a
range she chooses, and that can be replayed with a seed when someone asks
"why did job 17 start so late?"
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes four whole numbers:
  $1  SEED   starting seed for Bash's random generator
  $2  LOW    smallest allowed delay in minutes (may be negative or zero)
  $3  HIGH   largest allowed delay (HIGH is at least LOW)
  $4  COUNT  how many delays to print (at least 1)

First set RANDOM=$SEED so that the same arguments always give the same
output. Then print COUNT lines, each one

  slot=<n>

where n is a random whole number with LOW <= n <= HIGH, both ends included.
Build n from $RANDOM and the % operator. (HIGH - LOW + 1 is at most 1000.)

required_patterns.message: Draw the numbers from $RANDOM.
Squeeze $RANDOM into the range with the % operator.
Seed the generator first with RANDOM=<seed> so runs can be replayed.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use Bash's own $RANDOM.

test_cases.name: tiny range must reach every value

title: Sum, Min, Max
story:
Quarter-end. Gus has a file of daily bandwidth readings from the whole
cluster, one number per line, and wants to know the total, the quietest day
and the busiest day. He also wants the average, "but please don't tell me
it's 41.67, tell me 41, I've had enough decimals for one week." The file is
piped in, so your script gets exactly one chance to look at each number.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads whole numbers from standard input, one per
line (they may be negative; ignore blank lines). In a single pass print
exactly:

  count=<how many numbers>
  sum=<total>
  min=<smallest>
  max=<largest>
  avg=<sum / count, whole number, rounded toward zero>

If there are no numbers at all, print "no data" to stderr and exit with
status 1, printing nothing on stdout.

Do not use sort, awk, head or tail, and do not store the numbers in a file:
keep running totals in variables while you read.
concepts: initialising min and max from the first value

required_patterns.message: Read the numbers one by one with while read.

forbidden_patterns.message: Keep running totals in variables while you read, instead of reaching for another tool.

test_cases.name: negative numbers, smallest is below zero
all readings are bigger than zero, so min must not start at zero
all readings negative, so max must not start at zero

title: Rounding Division
story:
The harbour cluster costs the same amount every month, and Gus has to split
it between the customers who share it. Amounts are in cents, so no one can
pay half a cent. "Do I charge them 3 cents, or 4?" he asks about a bill that
divides into 3.5. Then: "And how many disks do I buy if each one holds 4
terabytes?" Same division, three different answers, depending on the
rounding. Time to get all three exactly right.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two whole numbers: AMOUNT ($1, zero or more) and
PARTS ($2, one or more). Print three lines:

  floor=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded down>
  nearest=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded to the nearest whole number; exactly .5 rounds UP>
  ceiling=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded up>

Examples: 7 / 2 = 3.5 gives floor 3, nearest 4, ceiling 4.
10 / 3 = 3.33 gives floor 3, nearest 3, ceiling 4. 8 / 4 = 2 gives 2, 2, 2.

If PARTS is 0, print "parts must be at least 1" to stderr and exit with
status 2. Use integer arithmetic only: no awk, no bc, no printf %.0f.

required_patterns.message: Do the divisions inside $(( )) with /.

forbidden_patterns.message: Rounding with integers only: add a little before you divide.
No floating point formats here: integers only.
